title: Mahayagya Ka Puraskaar
author: Yashpal
tagline: A hungry man gives his only four rotis to a starving dog — and discovers that this was his true great sacrifice.

overview.intro: Yashpal’s "Mahayagya Ka Puraskaar" ("The Reward of the Great Sacrifice") is a moral tale set in poverty. A once-prosperous Seth and his wife have fallen on hard times and can barely eat. On his wife’s suggestion, the Seth travels to Kunddanpur to sell the religious merit of a great yajna he once performed. On the road he meets a starving dog and gives it all four rotis packed for his journey. When he reaches the wealthy Dhanna Seth’s house, he is told that the only mahayagya worth buying is the one he performed that day — the feeding of a hungry creature. He refuses to sell it, and returns home to find treasure beneath his threshold.

learn.title: Poverty, and a plan to sell merit

blocks.text: The story begins in real hunger. A Seth who was once prosperous now struggles with his wife to find enough food, and the humiliation of the fall is as sharp as the hunger itself. In this world, the merit of religious acts is understood as something that can be transferred, bought and sold — so the Sethani’s suggestion is not sacrilege in her world but practical economy. If the merit of a great yajna can be sold, then past devotion can be converted into present bread.

The plan gives the story its irony from the very first page, because the reader is being asked to watch a man attempt to commercialise something sacred. Yashpal sets this trap carefully. We are not invited to condemn the Seth and his wife; poverty has made their reasoning understandable. That is precisely why the story’s later reversal lands with moral force rather than smugness.

learn.title: The road, the dog, and four rotis

items: Before leaving, the Seth obtains flour from a neighbour, and the Sethani prepares four rotis for his journey.
On the road to Kunddanpur he stops to rest and sees a starving, weak dog.
Moved by compassion, he gives the dog all four rotis and drinks water himself.
He reaches the house of the wealthy Dhanna Seth, whose wife is said to recognise genuine merit.
She offers to buy only the mahayagya he performed that day — which is the feeding of the dog.

blocks.text: The decisive act is quiet and unhesitating. The Seth has packed four rotis for a long journey and meets a creature with nothing; he gives all of them away and drinks water himself. There is no audience, no ritual and no expectation of reward, which is exactly what the story will later insist makes it a true sacrifice. The dog is not a test he passes deliberately — it is simply suffering, and he responds.

items.meaning: Once wealthy, now poor, and still compassionate; he gives away his food and refuses to sell his act of kindness.
His practical wife who proposes selling the merit of a past yajna so the couple can eat.
A wealthy woman credited with insight, who recognises the true mahayagya the Seth performed that day.
The starving creature whose need becomes the occasion for the story’s central moral act.
Provides the flour from which the Sethani makes the four rotis of the journey.

blocks.text: The cast is small and each figure carries an idea. The Seth and Sethani represent honest need; Dhanna Seth’s wife represents a wisdom that can see true merit; and the dog represents pure need with nothing to offer in return. That last quality is the point: giving to someone who can never repay you is what separates service from investment.

learn.title: The offer, the refusal and the reward

blocks.caption: Two kinds of sacrifice compared
rows: A grand ritual performed long ago
Four rotis given to a starving dog
The ritual, yes; the kindness, never

blocks.text: When Dhanna Seth’s wife names the day’s act as the real mahayagya, the Seth understands at once what she means — and refuses. Feeding a hungry creature, he feels, is a duty, not a commodity; to put a price on it would be to betray the act itself. He returns home empty-handed, and it is precisely then that treasure is found beneath the threshold of his house, presented as the reward of the selfless deed.

learn.title: Themes: duty, compassion and the limits of ritual

items.text: The Seth gives all four rotis and drinks only water.
items.note: Total, uncalculated giving — he keeps nothing back, which is what makes the act selfless rather than decorative.

items.text: He refuses to sell the day’s merit even when a buyer is ready.
items.note: The refusal defines the story’s ethic: compassion becomes false the moment it is priced.

items.text: Treasure is discovered beneath the threshold on his return.
items.note: The reward arrives unasked, after the deed is done and abandoned to itself.

blocks.text: The story’s central argument is that true service is measured by the sacrifice it costs and the motive it carries, not by ritual display. A secondary theme is the dignity of the poor, who in this tale retain moral greatness after losing wealth. Finally there is the idea that good deeds bear fruit — though the treasure is best read less as a literal jackpot and more as the story’s conviction that selflessness is never wasted.

The two questions this story reliably produces are on the central idea and on why the feeding of the dog counts as a mahayagya. Both are answered by the same logic: a great sacrifice is measured by what it costs the giver and by the absence of any motive of reward. Keep the contrast between the remembered ritual and the day’s compassionate act firmly in view, and use the four rotis as your concrete evidence.

items: Explain the world’s belief in transferable merit so the plan to sell it is understood, not mocked.
Use the four rotis to show the scale of the gift — it was all the food he had.
Close on the refusal: the moment the Seth declines to sell defines the story’s ethic.

keyPoints: The Seth and Sethani have fallen from prosperity into genuine hunger, which makes their plan understandable.
Their world allows religious merit to be transferred or sold, so selling a past yajna’s merit is practical, not merely profane.
The Sethani makes four rotis from a neighbour’s flour for the journey.
The decisive act: the Seth meets a starving dog and gives it all four rotis, drinking water himself.
There is no audience and no expected reward — the giving is uncalculated and complete.
Dhanna Seth’s wife identifies the feeding of the dog as the true mahayagya performed that day.
The Seth refuses to sell it, holding that helping a hungry creature is a duty, not a commodity.
He returns home empty-handed, and treasure is then found beneath the threshold — the unasked-for reward.
examFocus: Central idea: selfless service to a suffering creature is a greater sacrifice than any ritual performed for display or reward.
Why the dog’s meal is a mahayagya: it cost the giver all his food and carried no expectation of return.
The refusal defines the ethic — compassion is corrupted the moment it is given a price.

questions.prompt: What do the Seth and Sethani decide to sell?
options: The religious merit of a yajna the Seth once performed
questions.answer: The religious merit of a yajna the Seth once performed
questions.explanation: In their world, the merit of a yajna can be transferred or sold, so the Sethani suggests they sell the merit of one of his past great sacrifices to raise money for food.
questions.commonMistake: They sell merit, not property — the story is about commercialising a sacred act.

questions.prompt: How many rotis does the Sethani prepare for the journey?
questions.explanation: Using flour obtained from a neighbour, the Sethani makes four rotis for his journey — the entire stock of food he carries.
questions.commonMistake: Four rotis, and all of them are later given away.

questions.prompt: To whom does the Seth give his rotis on the road?
questions.explanation: Resting on the way to Kunddanpur, the Seth sees a starving, weak dog and, moved by compassion, gives it all four rotis, drinking water himself.
questions.commonMistake: The recipient is an animal with no status and no way to repay him.

questions.prompt: What does Dhanna Seth’s wife say she will buy?
options: Only the mahayagya he performed that day
The merit of his yajna from years ago
questions.answer: Only the mahayagya he performed that day
questions.explanation: She tells him that the only great sacrifice worth buying is the one he performed that day — the feeding of a hungry creature — which reveals her insight into true merit.
questions.commonMistake: She is not interested in the old ritual; she names the day’s compassionate act.

questions.prompt: What does the Seth do when he is offered money for the day’s merit?
questions.answer: He refuses the sale, holding that helping a hungry creature is a duty and not something to be sold.
questions.explanation: Though a buyer is ready and he returns home empty-handed, the Seth will not put a price on an act of compassion; to sell it would be to betray the deed itself.
questions.commonMistake: His refusal is principled, not a negotiation tactic or a change of mind.

questions.prompt: What is found when the Seth returns home?
questions.answer: A treasure is discovered beneath the threshold of his house, presented as the reward for his selfless act.
questions.explanation: He comes back without having sold anything, and treasure is then found under the threshold — the story’s sign that his compassion has borne fruit.
questions.commonMistake: The reward arrives after the deed and unasked, which is what makes it a reward rather than a payment.

questions.prompt: Why does Dhanna Seth’s wife call the feeding of a dog a mahayagya?
questions.answer: Because a true great sacrifice is measured by what it costs the giver and by the absence of any motive of reward. The Seth gave away all four rotis packed for his own long journey to a creature that could never repay him, keeping only water for himself, and he asked nothing in return. That combination of total cost and zero expectation, she implies, makes the act greater than any grand ritual performed with merit in view.
questions.explanation: A strong answer states the criterion (cost and motive), applies it to the four rotis and the powerless recipient, and contrasts it with ritual merit that is performed and priced.
questions.commonMistake: Do not say simply "because God rewarded it"; the story’s reasoning is about the nature of the gift.

questions.prompt: What does the Seth’s refusal to sell the merit show about his character?
questions.answer: It shows that his compassion is genuine and incorruptible — he will not commodify an act of kindness even when he badly needs the money.
questions.explanation: Poverty has made the couple’s plan understandable, but the refusal marks the limit the Seth will not cross: duty to a suffering creature cannot be turned into a transaction.
questions.commonMistake: Link the refusal to his poverty — it costs him real need, which is why it reveals character.

questions.prompt: Describe the Seth’s journey and explain the contrast the story draws between two kinds of sacrifice.
questions.answer: The once-prosperous Seth, now poor, sets out for Kunddanpur to sell the religious merit of a great yajna he once performed, hoping a wealthy buyer will recognise it. His wife packs four rotis made from a neighbour’s flour. On the road he rests and finds a starving, weak dog; moved by compassion, he gives the dog all four rotis and drinks only water. At Dhanna Seth’s house, he is told that the only mahayagya worth buying is the one he performed that day — the feeding of a hungry creature. He refuses to sell it and returns home empty-handed, where treasure is found beneath his threshold. The contrast is between a ritual performed with reward in view, whose merit is priced and traded, and an act of pure compassion given to one who can never repay. The story argues that the second is the greater sacrifice.
questions.explanation: Cover the plan, the four rotis, the dog, the offer, the refusal and the reward, then state the argument explicitly so the answer interprets the contrast rather than only telling the tale.
questions.commonMistake: Do not omit the refusal — it is the ethical centre of the story, not a minor detail.

questions.prompt: Do you think the treasure beneath the threshold is a fitting reward? Discuss.
questions.answer: The treasure is best read as the story’s conviction that selflessness is never wasted, rather than as a price placed on the deed. The Seth gave without any thought of return and had already accepted returning home empty-handed; the reward arrives after the act is complete and abandoned to itself, which preserves the purity of the giving. A reader today might find the ending too neat, but Yashpal’s purpose is moral rather than realistic: he wants to affirm that compassion bears fruit, and the buried treasure is his plainest way of saying so.
questions.explanation: This is a discussion question. Take a position, then support it with the timing of the reward (unasked and after the refusal) and the story’s didactic, fable-like form.
questions.commonMistake: Do not argue that the reward "pays for" the rotis; the story insists the act was a duty, never an investment.
